The Vapor Chamber Is Not the Heatsink​
A vapor chamber is often described as a cooling device.

More precisely, it is a two-dimensional heat-transport and heat-spreading structure placed between the hot semiconductor package and the final heat-rejection system.

The heat path is:

Die → TIM → package lid or heat spreader → vapor chamber → heatsink or cold plate → air or liquid

The vapor chamber does not create cooling by itself.

It moves heat away from a concentrated hot spot and distributes it across a much larger surface so the heatsink, fins, airflow, or liquid coolant can remove it more effectively.

From the outside, a vapor chamber may look like one thin copper plate.

Internally, however, it is a sealed structure containing:

a top copper wall;
a bottom copper wall;
a wick attached to one or both surfaces;
a small quantity of working fluid;
an internal vapor space;
support columns that prevent collapse under vacuum and mechanical pressure.

The thermal process begins at the hot region above the die.

Heat conducts through the lower copper wall and reaches the working fluid held inside the wick. The liquid evaporates, converting local heat into vapor.

That vapor rapidly spreads throughout the chamber toward cooler regions.

At those cooler surfaces, the vapor condenses and releases its heat into the copper wall. The heat then enters the heatsink, fins, or cold plate above the chamber.

The wick returns the condensed liquid to the hot region through capillary action, allowing the cycle to continue.

This creates a repeating loop:

Evaporation at the hot spot → vapor transport → condensation at cooler regions → liquid return through the wick

That is why a vapor chamber can spread heat more effectively than a simple solid copper plate.

A solid copper spreader relies only on conduction.

A vapor chamber combines conduction with phase-change heat transport.

The vapor chamber may be placed on top of a conventional integrated heat spreader, or it may replace the solid copper base of the heatsink. In compact systems, it may even contact the die through a thin thermal-interface material.

This means the vapor chamber can function as:

an additional heat spreader above the package;
the base of an air-cooled heatsink;
part of a liquid-cooling cold plate;
a direct-die thermal spreading structure.

For AI accelerators, GPUs, CPUs, and advanced heterogeneous packages, the importance of vapor chambers is increasing because heat generation is rarely uniform.

Hot spots may appear under compute chiplets, memory interfaces, optical engines, voltage regulators, or concentrated processing regions.

The cooling system must therefore do more than remove total power.

It must also control temperature non-uniformity.

But the vapor chamber introduces its own realization requirements.

Its performance depends on chamber thickness, wick design, working-fluid distribution, internal pressure, orientation, mechanical loading, surface flatness, attachment quality, TIM bond-line thickness, and contact with the heatsink.

Dry-out, wick limitation, internal deformation, poor contact, or non-uniform clamping can reduce performance even when the chamber itself is properly designed.

The most important point is simple:

The vapor chamber spreads and transports heat. The heatsink or cold plate ultimately removes it from the system.

The vapor chamber is not just another copper layer.

It is a sealed phase-change thermal system positioned directly inside the package-to-cooling realization path.
